chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muawiya ibn Ammar who said — he thinks from Abu Hamza al-Thumali — from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
Whenever the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) wanted to send out a military expedition (sariyya), he would call them and have them sit before him, then he would say:
'March in the name of God, and with God, and in the way of God, and upon the religion of the Messenger of God.

Do not commit excesses with the war gains, do not mutilate the dead, do not be treacherous, do not kill the decrepit elderly, nor a child, nor a woman, and do not cut down a tree unless you are compelled to do so.

And whichever man — from the lowest of the Muslims to the most virtuous among them — extends his protection toward a man from the polytheists, then that man is under protection until he hears the word of God. If he follows you, he is your brother in the faith; and if he refuses, then escort him to his place of safety, and seek assistance from God against him.'

key_terms.جَار: jar — neighbor or one under protection; in this context, an enemy combatant granted temporary safe conduct (aman)
key_terms.سَرِيَّة: sariyya — a military expedition or detachment sent out by the Prophet, typically without the Prophet himself leading
key_terms.غُلُول: ghulul — misappropriation or theft of war spoils before they are properly distributed; a grave sin in Islamic law
key_terms.كَلَام اللَّه: kalam Allah — the word/speech of God, i.e., the Quran, which the protected enemy is given the opportunity to hear
key_terms.مَأْمَن: ma'man — a place of safety; the enemy's homeland or territory where he will be safe
key_terms.مُثْلَة: muthla — mutilation of the dead; categorically forbidden

ai.seo_question: What were the Prophet Muhammad's rules of engagement for military expeditions according to al-Kafi?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) transmits the standing orders of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) for military expeditions (sariyya). These pre-battle instructions established a comprehensive code of conduct for warfare: prohibitions against misappropriating war spoils, mutilating the dead, treachery, and killing non-combatants (the elderly, children, women), as well as environmental protection. Remarkably, the Prophet also established that any Muslim — regardless of rank — could grant temporary protection (aman) to an enemy combatant, allowing him to hear the Quran before deciding whether to convert or return safely to his own territory. This hadith reflects the early Shia understanding that Islamic warfare is governed by strict ethical boundaries, distinguishing it from the tribal norms of pre-Islamic Arabia.
